content: Urinary catheterization is a frequently performed medical procedure, with approximately 15% to 25% of hospitalized patients requiring short-term indwelling urethral catheters (used for 14 days or less) during their care. However, the use of these catheters is associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs). Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) are among the most common hospital-acquired infections. It is estimated that around 20% of hospital-acquired bloodstream infections (bacteraemias) originate from the urinary tract, with an associated mortality rate of approximately 10%. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of different strategies for removing short-term indwelling urethral catheters in adults. The evidence was gathered from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that assessed the effectiveness of various practices for catheter removal in any setting. A total of 99 trials involving 12,241 participants were included in the analysis. Most of the trials were judged to have a low or unclear risk of selection and detection bias, but a high risk of performance bias. Attrition and reporting biases were generally low. None of the trials reported on the quality of life of participants. Thirteen trials involving 1,506 participants compared the removal of catheters at different times of the day. Specifically, early morning removal (between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m.) was compared to late-night removal (between 10 p.m. and midnight). The evidence suggests that removing catheters late at night may slightly reduce the need for recatheterization compared to early morning removal (relative risk [RR] 0.71, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53 to 0.96; low-certainty evidence). However, it is uncertain whether the time of removal affects the risk of developing symptomatic CAUTI (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.63; very low-certainty evidence) or the risk of experiencing dysuria (RR 2.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 6.86; low-certainty evidence). Sixty-eight trials involving 9,247 participants compared shorter versus longer durations of catheterization. Shorter durations of catheter use may increase the likelihood of requiring recatheterization compared to longer durations (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.41; low-certainty evidence). However, shorter durations probably reduce the risk of symptomatic CAUTI (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.61; moderate-certainty evidence) and may reduce the risk of dysuria (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.88; low-certainty evidence). Seven trials involving 714 participants compared catheter clamping policies to free drainage. The evidence suggests that there may be little to no difference between clamping and free drainage in terms of the risk of requiring recatheterization (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.21; low-certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether clamping versus free drainage affects the risk of symptomatic CAUTI (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.63; very low-certainty evidence) or dysuria (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.54; very low-certainty evidence). Three trials involving 402 participants investigated the use of prophylactic alpha-blockers before catheter removal compared to no intervention or placebo. The evidence is very uncertain about whether alpha-blockers reduce the risk of requiring recatheterization (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.42; very low-certainty evidence) or the risk of symptomatic CAUTI (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.06; very low-certainty evidence). None of the trials on alpha-blockers reported data on the occurrence of dysuria. In conclusion, there is some evidence to suggest that removing indwelling urethral catheters late at night rather than early in the morning may reduce the need for recatheterization. Shorter durations of catheter use probably reduce the risk of symptomatic CAUTI and may reduce the risk of dysuria, but they may also increase the likelihood of recatheterization. The evidence regarding other strategies, such as clamping versus free drainage or the use of prophylactic alpha-blockers, is too uncertain to draw definitive conclusions. The low certainty of much of the evidence highlights the need for further research, which could significantly impact clinical practice. Future studies should include standardized outcome measures and investigate the effects of catheter removal strategies in non-surgical patients.
